summary: In Greek mythology, the Keres (Κῆρες) were female death-spirits who personified violent death. As daughters of the primordial goddess Nyx (Night), they were drawn to bloody deaths on the battlefield, hovering over the dying and wounded to feed on the slain. They could not themselves kill, but waited for death to come and consumed the blood of the fallen.
etymology: The Greek noun kēr (κήρ) means "death" or "doom," appearing in both the singular (Κήρ) and the plural (Κῆρες). Homer uses the phrase "keres of death," and the word could extend metaphorically to a person's individual fate or doom.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: The Keres were daughters of Nyx (Night). Hesiod groups them among Nyx's brood of dark powers alongside Thanatos (Death), the Moirai (the Fates), Hypnos (Sleep), the Oneiroi (Dreams), Nemesis, Eris (Strife), and Geras (Old Age).
Later authorities varied the genealogy. Cicero, using the Latin name Tenebrae ("the Darknesses"), described them as the daughters of Erebus (Darkness) and Nyx rather than of Nyx alone.

sections.heading: Role and function
paragraphs: The Keres personified violent death and were associated above all with the slaughter of the battlefield. Ancient sources depict them as dark beings with gnashing teeth and claws, thirsting for human blood, who hovered over the fighting in search of the dying and the wounded.

They held no power of death in themselves; they could only wait for death to strike and then drink the blood of the slain. By extension, the word kēr also came to express the personal fate or doom that awaited each individual.

sections.heading: In literature
paragraphs: Hesiod names the Keres among the children of Night in the Theogony. The pseudo-Hesiodic Shield of Heracles describes the dark Dooms gnashing their white teeth as they fought over the dying, one of them clasping her great claws around a fallen man as his soul went down to Hades.

Homer refers to the Keres as countless in number and depicts them, alongside other personifications, on the Shield of Achilles in the Iliad. The later poet Quintus Smyrnaeus, in his Posthomerica, mentions twin Keres, one dark and one bright.

sections.heading: Cult
paragraphs: The Keres figured in Athenian ritual during the festival of the Anthesteria. At its close, the spirits were ritually driven away through apotropaic rites and purification ceremonies intended to keep them at bay.
